sections.heading: Purpose and intended use
sections.text: The IFRS 9 SICR and Staging model (MDL-09, model version 2.2) allocates every financial instrument within the IFRS 9 impairment scope to Stage 1, Stage 2 or Stage 3 at each monthly reporting date, and thereby determines whether the loss allowance is measured at 12-month or lifetime expected credit losses. Stage 2 is assigned to every instrument whose credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition, so that lifetime ECL is recognised for these instruments, and Stage 1 is assigned where no such increase has occurred, so that the loss allowance is measured at 12-month ECL. The model is a quantitative method whose output is used for financial reporting and is therefore managed as a model under the Model Risk Management Policy across its full lifecycle, although its core consists of deterministic rules calibrated with expert judgement. It was developed internally by IFRS 9 Modelling and is managed under the Model Risk Management Policy; no vendor component is used. The intended uses are stage allocation for the IFRS 9 loss allowance, the stage breakdown in FINREP and the IFRS 7 disclosures, and, as secondary uses, the Stage 2 ratio in the credit risk appetite dashboard and the identification of Stage 2 exposures in the ICAAP credit risk projections.

sections.heading: Scope of application
sections.text: The model covers financial assets at amortised cost and at fair value through other comprehensive income, lease receivables, loan commitments and financial guarantee contracts of the Bank N.V., its consumer credit subsidiary and its Belgian branch, with a gross carrying amount of EUR 186.2 billion and off-balance exposures of EUR 21.7 billion at 31 December 2026. The portfolios in scope are residential mortgages (EUR 121.6 billion, 548,000 facilities), consumer lending (EUR 6.8 billion, 1.42 million facilities), retail SME (EUR 14.2 billion, 191,000 facilities), corporates (EUR 31.5 billion, 24,600 facilities) and financial institutions, sovereigns and debt securities (EUR 12.1 billion, 1,420 facilities). At 31 December 2026, 88.9% of the gross carrying amount was in Stage 1 (EUR 165.5 billion), 9.4% in Stage 2 (EUR 17.5 billion) and 1.7% in Stage 3 (EUR 3.2 billion), with loss allowances of EUR 212 million, EUR 418 million and EUR 890 million respectively. Purchased or originated credit-impaired assets (EUR 41 million) are identified at initial recognition and are not staged; their loss allowance comprises only the cumulative changes in lifetime ECL since initial recognition. Trade receivables and contract assets under the simplified approach are measured by Finance outside the model and are out of scope.

sections.heading: Users and regulatory use
sections.text: The principal users are Group Reporting and Impairment (Finance), which books the loss allowance, Credit Risk Management, which maintains the watchlist and forbearance inputs and reviews stage overrides, and Risk Reporting, which reports Stage 2 and Stage 3 ratios to the Group Risk Committee. The regulatory use is IFRS 9 financial reporting, including the stage breakdown in FINREP templates F 18.00 and F 12.01; the model is not used for own funds requirements. Stage allocation is not used to take decisions on individual customers: the Privacy Office concluded in DPIA-2024-061 that stage allocation has no legal or similarly significant effect on data subjects, so no automated individual decision within the meaning of Art. 22 GDPR is taken, and the Stage 2 flag does not play a determining role in any customer decision. Known limitations of the model, the conditions of approval and the collective transfers in force are communicated quarterly to Finance and Credit Risk Management through the staging factsheet. The model's Stage 2 ratio is one of the credit risk appetite metrics; the risk parameters behind it are produced by models registered in the model inventory and approved under MRM-POL-001.

sections.heading: Model structure and stage allocation hierarchy
sections.text: Stage allocation is performed monthly at facility level by the staging module of the IFRS 9 calculation engine (ICE), in the following order: (1) POCI assets are excluded from staging; (2) exposures in default under CR-STD-110 are allocated to Stage 3; (3) performing exposures meeting any Stage 2 criterion are allocated to Stage 2; (4) all other exposures are allocated to Stage 1. The Stage 2 criteria are the quantitative lifetime PD criterion (section 4.3), more than 30 days past due on a material amount, forborne performing status, watchlist status, the low credit risk assessment for debt securities, collective Stage 2 transfers and approved manual stage overrides. The criteria combine forward-looking PD information, borrower-specific qualitative information from Credit Risk Management and past-due information, weighted by their relevance for each portfolio through the order of the hierarchy and the portfolio-specific thresholds, so that the assessment is multifactor rather than based on a single indicator. The SICR assessment is performed on the risk of default before the effect of collateral or guarantees; collateral affects the ECL measurement through LGD but not the stage. The model design distinguishes the definition of SICR per exposure type in a clear, documented policy approved by the Group Impairment Committee as part of FIN-STD-200.

sections.heading: Stage 3, credit-impaired assets and definition of default
sections.text: Stage 3 comprises all exposures in default under the prudential definition of default of CR-STD-110, which implements Article 178 CRR, Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 and EBA/GL/2016/07; the IFRS 9 definition of default is therefore identical to the definition used for internal credit risk management. Default is presumed no later than 90 days past due for all portfolios; the Bank does not use a more lagging criterion for any instrument. Credit-impaired assets are identified from observable evidence of events with a detrimental impact on estimated future cash flows, such as significant financial difficulty, a breach of contract or past-due event, concessions granted for reasons of financial difficulty and probable bankruptcy, including the combined effect of several events, all of which are default triggers under CR-STD-110. Stage 3 exposures above EUR 1 million per obligor are measured by the workout function as the difference between the gross carrying amount and the present value of the estimated future cash flows discounted at the original effective interest rate; other Stage 3 exposures use time-in-default LGD models. Definitions of the key terms default, credit-impaired, SICR, Stage 2 and cure are listed in Annex 1 of this document; they are identical for accounting, capital and credit risk management purposes, so no reconciliation of differing definitions is required.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models
sections.text: The model depends on the IFRS 9 PD term structures of the ECL models for residential mortgages (MDL-07), corporates (MDL-08), consumer lending and retail SME, and on the macroeconomic scenarios and probability weights produced by the Macroeconomic Scenario and Satellite Models (MDL-10). The current lifetime PD is the probability-weighted PD over the baseline, upside and downside scenarios approved quarterly by the Group Impairment Committee, so that forward-looking information enters the staging assessment through the PD term structures. The same scenarios and the same PD term structures are used for staging and measurement, and the Stage 2 population is also used in the ICAAP credit risk projections, so that the forward-looking information is consistent across financial reporting, capital planning and management information. The default flag, forbearance status and watchlist status are inputs maintained by Credit Risk Management under CR-STD-110 and CR-POL-001. Upstream model changes are notified to the model owner through the inventory dependency register, and a change of an upstream PD model triggers an assessment of the SICR thresholds.

sections.heading: Segmentation
sections.text: Thresholds are set per portfolio (residential mortgages, consumer lending, retail SME, corporates including financial institutions) and, within each portfolio, per origination PD band, because the significance of a given change in default risk depends on the default risk at initial recognition. The origination PD bands are, for mortgages and corporates, below 0.25% (corporates 0.5%), up to 1.0% (corporates 2.0%) and above; for consumer lending below 1.0%, 1.0% to 3.0% and above; and for retail SME below 1.0% and above. The grouping on portfolio, product and origination PD band is granular enough to assess changes in credit risk: the stage is determined per facility, and the groups are used only to set thresholds, so that group performance cannot obscure increases in credit risk of individual exposures. The segmentation was set by expert judgement EJ-09-01 and confirmed by the calibration results of chapter 5.

sections.heading: Loan commitments, financial guarantees and modifications
sections.text: For loan commitments and financial guarantee contracts, the date on which the Bank became party to the irrevocable commitment is the date of initial recognition, and the origination PD stored at that date is the reference point for the SICR assessment of the commitment and of the drawn exposure that results from it. For modified financial assets that are not derecognised, the risk of default at the reporting date under the modified terms is compared with the risk of default at initial recognition under the original, unmodified terms, which ORIG_RISK retains. The gross carrying amount of such assets is recalculated by Finance as the present value of the modified contractual cash flows discounted at the original effective interest rate, and the modification gain or loss is recognised in profit or loss; the staging model uses the recalculated amount. A modification is not taken as evidence of lower credit risk: modified exposures that are forborne remain in Stage 2 for at least the two-year forborne-performing probation period and return to Stage 1 only after a history of timely payments against the modified terms. The gross carrying amount is written off when there is no reasonable expectation of recovery under the write-off policy of Finance; written-off amounts leave the staging population and the write-off data used in back-testing are consistent with that policy.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: The calibration and back-testing data are described in the approved RDS documentation STG-RDS v3.0 (document version 1.0 of 5 March 2027), and the frozen RDS version STG-RDS-v3.0-20270212 is used for all results in this document. The RDS contains 44 quarterly reference dates from March 2015 to December 2025 with twelve-month outcomes up to December 2026, 88.7 million facility-quarter observations and 301,420 default events. The data include information on past events (arrears, defaults, forbearance), current conditions (current PDs and watchlist status) and forecasts (scenario-conditional PD term structures), considered using experienced credit judgement of IFRS 9 Modelling and Credit Risk Management to determine which information is reasonable and supportable. The data were subject to a data quality assessment concluding that they are fit for use, and the data deficiencies DD-09-01 to DD-09-05 are cross-referenced to the limitations log in section 8.2.

sections.heading: Calibration, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples
sections.text: The samples were defined in the development plan before calibration started: the calibration sample contains the reference dates March 2015 to December 2022 excluding the moratoria quarters (June 2020 to March 2021), the out-of-sample test is a random 30% hold-out of obligors from the same period, and the out-of-time sample contains the reference dates March 2023 to December 2025. The out-of-time sample was not used for the selection of the origination PD bands or for threshold calibration. The samples contain, respectively, 51.2 million, 21.9 million and 15.6 million observations with 176,480, 75,630 and 49,310 default events. The data evaluated cover eleven years, and the historical relationship between PD ratios and defaults is adjusted for current and forecast conditions because the PD term structures themselves are point-in-time and scenario-conditional.

sections.heading: Alternatives considered
sections.text: Four methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (compliance with IFRS 9 and FIN-STD-200, data availability, early default capture, stage stability, interpretability and implementation constraints): (A) relative change in annualised remaining lifetime PD combined with an absolute PD floor; (B) a downgrade of at least three notches on the Bank's master scale; (C) the relative change in 12-month PD only; (D) a statistical transfer model estimating the probability of default within twelve months from the PD ratio, arrears and behavioural variables. Alternative B does not compare risk on a consistent remaining-life basis and is insensitive to forward-looking information for retail pools; alternative C is not compliant with FIN-STD-200 §5.2 for amortising mortgages where default risk is not evenly distributed over the life. Alternative D achieved a two-percentage-point higher capture rate on the out-of-time sample but is less transparent, requires a separate model for each portfolio and would combine a statistical score with stage allocation in a way that is difficult to explain in IFRS 7 disclosures.

sections.heading: Selection rationale
sections.text: Alternative A was selected because it implements the comparison of lifetime default risk required by IFRS 9 paragraph 5.5.9 and FIN-STD-200 §5.2 and §5.3, is transparent, reuses the approved PD term structures and produces stage outcomes that can be reproduced facility by facility. The less transparent alternative D was rejected because its performance gain of two percentage points in capture rate is not sufficient to justify the additional complexity and controls. The three-notch downgrade rule (alternative B) is retained as a benchmark in section 7.4, and the 12-month PD proxy (alternative C) is used only where the conditions of section 4.4 are met. The model is thus a threshold rule applied to model-based PDs; it is not a statistical model with estimated coefficients, and chapter 4 of the template is applied accordingly.

sections.heading: Primary quantitative criterion
sections.text: The SICR assessment performed at each reporting date is based on the change in the risk of a default occurring over the expected life of the instrument, not on the change in the amount of expected credit losses. For each facility, the annualised remaining lifetime PD at the reporting date, PD_cur = 1 − (1 − cumPD_cur(T))^(1/T), is compared with the annualised lifetime PD that was expected at initial recognition for the same remaining term T, PD_orig, taken from the origination PD term structure stored in ORIG_RISK. Comparing annualised PDs for the same remaining term removes the effect of the passage of time on lifetime default risk, so that risk at the reporting date is not simply compared in absolute terms with risk at origination. Both PD_cur and PD_orig are probability-weighted over the macroeconomic scenarios; PD_orig uses the scenarios in force at the origination date. A SICR is identified when the ratio PD_cur/PD_orig exceeds the relative threshold of the portfolio and origination PD band and, in addition, PD_cur − PD_orig exceeds the absolute threshold of the portfolio. The relative change is measured as the ratio of the current to the origination PD, and the absolute change as the difference in percentage points, so both the relative and the absolute change in PD are taken into consideration.

sections.heading: Use of 12-month PD for revolving consumer facilities
sections.text: For credit cards and overdrafts, which have no contractual maturity and a behavioural life of 36 months determined by the consumer lending EAD model, the ratio of current to origination 12-month PD is used as a proxy for the ratio of lifetime PDs. The evidence that the proxy is not materially different from the lifetime comparison will be added after the 2026 back-testing. The behavioural life used for the lifetime PD of revolving facilities is estimated from historical account behaviour and not the one-month contractual notice period.

sections.heading: Relative and absolute thresholds
sections.text: The relative thresholds decrease with the origination PD band, because a given absolute change in the risk of default is more significant for an instrument originated with a lower risk of default than for one originated with a higher risk. The absolute threshold prevents transfers caused by immaterial PD movements of low-PD exposures, and together with the relative threshold ensures that SICR is not equated with a statistically significant change in PD. Thresholds are calibrated per portfolio as set out in chapter 5, and the threshold values themselves are stored as a version-controlled parameter table in the ICE configuration. The thresholds are applied to all exposures of a portfolio individually; the stage of a facility is therefore not affected by the performance of other facilities in the same group.

sections.heading: Qualitative criteria and backstops
sections.text: Irrespective of the quantitative criterion, the following backstops allocate a performing exposure to Stage 2: more than 30 days past due on a material amount; forborne performing status, for at least the two-year forborne-performing probation period; and inclusion of the obligor on the watchlist. The rebuttable presumption that credit risk has increased significantly when contractual payments are more than 30 days past due is applied to all portfolios as the latest point of transfer, and it is not rebutted for any portfolio. Because the presumption is not rebutted, no analysis demonstrating the absence of correlation between 30 days past due and SICR has been performed or is required; a rebuttal would require a dispensation under FIN-STD-200 §14 supported by such an analysis. The 30 days past due backstop is used alongside the earlier PD, watchlist and forbearance indicators and not as the primary indicator: in 2026 only 9.8% of defaulted facilities had reached Stage 2 through the backstop alone. The watchlist criterion reflects the early-warning indicators of CR-POL-001 §10.1, which include covenant breaches, significant changes in the borrower's operating results, external rating downgrades and adverse sector information, and therefore captures qualitative indicators of increased credit risk that the PD does not reflect. The SICR assessment is not based solely on quantitative analysis.

sections.heading: Collective assessment and collective Stage 2 transfers
sections.text: Where evidence of a significant increase in credit risk is not yet available at facility level, SICR is assessed collectively for groups of exposures sharing credit risk characteristics, using information indicative of increased credit risk for those groups. Each collective transfer specifies the affected population, the triggering evidence and its review date, and is approved by the Group Impairment Committee together with the associated overlay. Collective transfer CST-2025-01 transfers to Stage 2 the interest-only residential mortgages with an indexed loan-to-value above 80% and a contractual maturity before 2037 (EUR 2.4 billion, 21,300 facilities), because refinancing risk at maturity is not reflected in the behavioural PD; it corresponds to overlay OVL-2025-02 of EUR 11.8 million, so that stage allocation and measurement are consistent. Where a sub-group with increased credit risk cannot be identified precisely, the transfer is applied to the portion of the group for which credit risk is deemed to have increased significantly, as delimited by the loan-to-value and maturity criteria. No other collective transfer is in force at 31 December 2026; the transfer CST-2022-02 for energy-intensive corporate sectors was withdrawn on 30 September 2024.

sections.heading: Low credit risk exemption
sections.text: The low credit risk exemption is applied only to debt securities with an internal rating equivalent to investment grade (internal grades 1 to 10 on the 22-grade master scale, equivalent to BBB− or better) and is not applied to loans and advances. The internal rating reflects a low risk of default and a strong capacity of the issuer to meet its contractual cash flow obligations in the near term, assessed without reliance on collateral and not merely relative to other exposures of the Bank or to the issuer's jurisdiction. Low credit risk is evaluated primarily on the internal rating; an external investment-grade rating does not qualify an instrument automatically, and where the internal rating is more favourable than the external rating the difference is justified in the credit file. At 31 December 2026 the exemption applies to 318 debt securities with a carrying amount of EUR 9.4 billion, all rated in internal grades 1 to 6. A debt security that ceases to qualify as low credit risk is not transferred to Stage 2 automatically; the quantitative criterion is then applied against its PD at initial recognition.

sections.heading: Transfer back to Stage 1 and exit from Stage 3
sections.text: An exposure returns from Stage 2 to Stage 1 when none of the Stage 2 criteria is met at the reporting date, so that the loss allowance is again measured at 12-month ECL; no probation applies beyond the forborne-performing probation period. Exposures leave Stage 3 only after completion of the probation period defined in CR-STD-110 (three months, or twelve months after a distressed restructuring), after which they are allocated to Stage 2 if they are forborne performing or meet another Stage 2 criterion. A decrease in allowance following a renegotiation or modification requires a consistently satisfactory payment performance over the forborne-performing probation period of at least two years. The effectiveness of this symmetrical treatment is monitored through the stage reversal KPI of section 10.1: in 2026, 17.3% of facilities transferred to Stage 2 returned to Stage 1 within six months.

sections.heading: Origination PD for legacy facilities
sections.text: For facilities originated before origination PDs were stored (mortgages before 2008, retail SME before 2012, corporates before 2010), the origination PD is proxied by the PD of the earliest archived rating adjusted to the origination date with the average migration between origination and first rating (EJ-09-03). Legacy facilities represent 14.8% of mortgage, 9.6% of retail SME and 3.1% of corporate facilities at 31 December 2026. The impact of the proxy on stage allocation was analysed against an alternative proxy without migration adjustment: the Stage 2 share of legacy facilities changes from 7.1% to 7.6% for mortgages and from 9.9% to 10.4% for retail SME, with a combined impact on the loss allowance of EUR 3.0 million. The proxy is recorded as limitation LIM-09-04 and its share declines by roughly one percentage point per year as legacy facilities mature.

sections.heading: Calibration target and method
sections.text: The calibration target is the trade-off between early default capture and stage volatility: for each portfolio and origination PD band, a grid of relative thresholds (1.25 to 4.0 in steps of 0.05) and absolute thresholds (0.05 to 2.0 percentage points in steps of 0.05) is evaluated on the calibration sample. For each grid point the capture rate (share of defaults allocated to Stage 2 at least six months before default), the Stage 2 share of the performing gross carrying amount and the stage reversal rate are computed. The selected thresholds lie at the point of the trade-off curve beyond which one additional percentage point of Stage 2 share adds less than one percentage point of capture rate, subject to a stage reversal rate below 25%; this knee-point rule is expert judgement EJ-09-06. The calibration is re-assessed at least annually during the annual model review.

sections.heading: Calibrated thresholds
sections.text: The thresholds in force from model version 2.2 are as follows. Residential mortgages: relative threshold 3.0 for origination PD below 0.25%, 2.5 from 0.25% to below 1.0% and 2.0 from 1.0%, with an absolute threshold of 0.20 percentage points. Consumer lending: relative threshold 2.25 for origination PD below 1.0%, 1.9 from 1.0% to below 3.0% and 1.6 from 3.0%, with an absolute threshold of 0.75 percentage points (0.0075 in PD units). Retail SME: relative threshold 2.5 for origination PD below 1.0% and 2.0 from 1.0%, with an absolute threshold of 0.50 percentage points; corporates and financial institutions: relative threshold 3.0 below 0.5%, 2.5 from 0.5% to below 2.0% and 2.0 from 2.0%, with an absolute threshold of 0.40 percentage points. On the calibration sample these thresholds capture 72.8% (mortgages), 64.1% (consumer lending), 65.0% (retail SME) and 67.9% (corporates) of defaults at least six months before default, at Stage 2 shares of 6.3%, 12.6%, 10.2% and 8.8% of the performing gross carrying amount. The mortgage, retail SME and corporate thresholds were re-assessed quantitatively in 2027 and remain unchanged from version 2.0, because the knee point moved by less than one grid step.

sections.heading: Margin of conservatism
sections.text: Not applicable. The staging model produces an unbiased stage allocation for IFRS 9 purposes, and FIN-STD-200 §4.1 excludes prudential conservatism from IFRS 9 models: no margin of conservatism, downturn component or regulatory floor is applied to the thresholds or to the PD inputs used for staging. Where the upstream PD term structures are derived from IRB parameters, the removal of MoC and downturn components and the TTC-to-PIT conversion are documented, justified and quantified in the MDDs of the PD models, and the staging model uses only the resulting IFRS 9 PDs. Uncertainty in the thresholds is addressed through the sensitivity analysis of section 7.5 and, where a risk is not captured, through overlays under FIN-STD-200 §10 rather than conservatism in the thresholds.

sections.heading: Performance metrics and thresholds
sections.text: Performance is measured on the calibration, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples by the capture rate (discriminatory power of the staging rule for defaults six or more months ahead), the Stage 1 direct-to-default share, the backstop-only share, the stage reversal rate and the population stability of the SICR ratio. The acceptance thresholds, set in the monitoring plan and approved by MRM because MV-HB-003 contains no specific staging tests, are: capture rate green from 60%, amber from 45%; Stage 1 direct-to-default green up to 25%, amber up to 35%; backstop-only share green up to 15%, amber up to 25%; stage reversal green up to 25%, amber up to 35%; PSI green below 0.10 and red above 0.25. The discriminatory power of the SICR ratio for defaults in the following twelve months, measured by the AUC, is 0.84 for mortgages, 0.79 for consumer lending, 0.77 for retail SME and 0.74 for corporates on the out-of-time sample, compared with 0.85, 0.80, 0.78 and 0.75 on the calibration sample. Where performance thresholds are significantly breached, the monitoring plan requires remedial action up to recalibration of the thresholds or redevelopment of the staging rule.

sections.heading: Staging back-testing results
sections.text: Back-testing of stage allocation is performed annually on the defaults of the preceding calendar year. For defaults in 2026, the share of defaulted facilities that were in Stage 2 at least six months before default was 71.4% for mortgages, 58.2% for consumer lending, 63.5% for retail SME and 66.7% for corporates, 59.5% in total by count; 22.4% of defaults came directly from Stage 1 and 9.8% had reached Stage 2 through the 30 days past due backstop alone. The frequency of stage reversals, measured as the share of Stage 2 inflows returning to Stage 1 within six months, was 17.3%. The amber consumer lending result was analysed for its cause (portfolio shift towards lower origination PDs), recorded as limitation LIM-09-11 and addressed by the recalibration of section 5.3; with the recalibrated thresholds the 2026 consumer capture rate would have been 64.9%. The back-test results are consistent with the direction of observable data: the Stage 2 share increased from 8.7% to 9.4% in 2026 as unemployment rose from 3.7% to 4.1% and arrears in consumer lending increased.

sections.heading: Benchmarking
sections.text: As a Tier 2 model, the staging model is compared with two benchmarks: the previous model version 2.1 and the three-notch downgrade rule (alternative B). On the 2023–2025 out-of-time sample, version 2.2 captures 66.1% of defaults six months ahead with a Stage 2 share of 9.1%, version 2.1 captures 64.4% at 8.8% and the three-notch rule 57.3% at 7.9%. The difference to the three-notch rule arises mainly in retail portfolios, where master-scale notches are coarse and the rule ignores the scenario-dependent PD term structure; the benchmark does not outperform the model on any material metric. The statistical transfer model (alternative D) captured 68.1% at a Stage 2 share of 9.3%, a difference that is explained in section 4.1 and does not justify its complexity.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions, parameters and input data: thresholds shifted by one grid step up and down, the calibration window with and without the 2015 approximated defaults and the moratoria quarters, the alternative legacy origination PD proxy, and the 12-month PD proxy for revolving facilities. A shift of all relative thresholds by +0.25 reduces the Stage 2 share from 9.4% to 8.3% and the loss allowance by EUR 38 million; a shift by −0.25 increases them to 10.8% and by EUR 47 million. Including the moratoria quarters in the calibration objective would raise the selected consumer relative threshold in the middle band from 1.9 to 2.0 and reduce the loss allowance by EUR 2.1 million; excluding the 2015 reference dates changes no threshold. Under a 100% weight on the downside scenario of MDL-10 the Stage 2 share rises to 13.1% and the loss allowance by EUR 108 million, and under a 100% weight on the upside scenario the Stage 2 share falls to 7.8% and the loss allowance by EUR 84 million, which demonstrates how stage allocation and ECL change with the scenarios. Because the calibration window contains no severe housing downturn, a stress test of the mortgage thresholds on the 2009–2013 approximated data shows a capture rate of 69%, close to the calibration result.

sections.heading: Consistency with ECL measurement and loss experience
sections.text: The ECL measurement method for each portfolio is the PD/LGD/EAD approach of the respective ECL model, with discounted cash flows for individually assessed Stage 3 exposures; the staging model determines only whether 12-month or lifetime ECL is measured. Twelve-month ECL is measured as the lifetime cash shortfalls resulting from a default within twelve months after the reporting date weighted by that default probability, not as the cash shortfalls expected over the next twelve months; the staging flag selects the corresponding PD horizon in ICE. ECL is calculated separately per scenario and probability-weighted, which reflects both the possibility that a credit loss occurs and the possibility that none occurs, and is discounted to the reporting date at the effective interest rate. The annual review compares the loss allowance of Stage 2 exposures with realised credit losses and write-offs; the methodology and thresholds are reviewed to reduce differences between estimates and loss experience. The ECL horizon for Stage 2 facilities does not exceed the maximum contractual period, including extension options, except for revolving facilities, for which the behavioural period of section 4.4 applies.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: All material assumptions were identified and assessed for plausibility: (a) the PD term structures of the upstream models are accurate and point-in-time; (b) the relationship between PD ratio and subsequent default observed in 2015–2025 remains stable; (c) watchlist and forbearance flags are complete and timely; (d) the origination PD proxy for legacy facilities is unbiased; (e) the 12-month PD ratio is a reasonable proxy for revolving facilities. Assumption (a) is supported by the annual back-testing of the PD models, (b) by the stable AUC between calibration and out-of-time samples, (c) by the DQ results in the RDS documentation, (d) by the sensitivity analysis of section 4.10 and (e) by the agreement analysis of section 4.4. The staging model assumes that credit risk management actions such as limit reductions do not mitigate ECL within the behavioural life, consistent with the EAD model.

sections.heading: Implementation specification and handover

The handover package to Finance Risk IT contained the implementation specification, the final threshold table, 1,240 test cases with expected stage outcomes produced with the development code, covering typical cases, boundary values at each threshold, missing and invalid inputs and every portfolio and origination PD band, and reference outputs for the full portfolio at 31 December 2026. The development and production lineage were compared: both read the same FRDP tables, and the difference in the legacy product mapping has no effect on outputs.

sections.heading: Production controls
sections.text: Production and development code are held in the approved version control system; the staging module is released from the repository ifrs9/ice-staging with tag 2.2.0, and the threshold table is a version-controlled, access-restricted parameter file changed only through change management. Model developers in IFRS 9 Modelling have read-only access to the production environment; deployments are performed by Finance Risk IT after four-eyes code review by a person other than the author and documented approval. Each production run logs the reference date, the input data version, the code version and the parameter table version, and the engine refuses to start if the parameter version differs from the approved version in the release register. Manual reruns and the fallback allocation to Stage 2 for facilities without a current PD are documented in the run book, authorised by the Head of Impairment Reporting and logged. Stage outputs used for regulatory reporting are retained for ten years together with the input data and code version used to produce them.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan and KPIs
sections.text: The monitoring plan MP-09 v3.0, approved by the model owner on 21 May 2027 and reviewed by Model Validation on 10 May 2027, is part of this chapter. Monitoring is performed quarterly, which exceeds the semi-annual minimum for Tier 2 models, and results are finalised within 45 calendar days after the quarter end. The KPIs, computed for the whole model and for each portfolio and origination PD band, are: K1 capture rate (green from 60%, amber from 45%, red below 45%); K2 Stage 1 direct-to-default share (green up to 25%, red above 35%); K3 backstop-only share (green up to 15%, red above 25%); K4 stage reversal rate (green up to 25%, red above 35%); K5 PSI of the SICR ratio and of the origination PD band distribution (0.10/0.25); K6 coverage (share of facilities with fallback allocation or proxied origination PD, green below 0.5% fallback); K7 stage override rate (green up to 2%, red above 5%); K8 production DQ results; and K9 overlays and collective transfers in place. The KPIs were set because MV-HB-003 does not define staging-specific tests; they measure discriminatory power, stability, data quality, overrides, overlays and coverage. The plan is updated whenever the model changes and reviewed at least annually; version 3.0 adds the band-level K1 reporting.

sections.heading: Escalation and reporting
sections.text: Each amber KPI is analysed by the model owner and its cause documented in the monitoring report; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive quarters, is notified to MRM and Model Validation within ten business days, followed by a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 calendar days. The action plan proposes no action with justification, a temporary overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or a restriction of use, and changes are processed under MRM-STD-050. A red outcome is also assessed against FIN-STD-200 §12.3, requiring a remediation plan approved by the Model Risk Committee within three months and an assessment of the need for a temporary overlay. The quarterly monitoring report shows each KPI with value, threshold, traffic light and trend over the last four quarters, the override rates by direction, reason and approving unit, the overlays in place with amount and planned removal date, and model coverage. The report is sent to Finance and to Credit Risk Management; monitoring code and data are version-controlled in ifrs9/stg-monitoring so that results are reproducible.

sections.heading: Materiality, challenge and approval
sections.text: Each judgement is classified by its impact on the loss allowance and on the share of exposures changing stage relative to the output without the judgement or the best statistical alternative; EJ-09-01, EJ-09-02, EJ-09-05 and EJ-09-06 are medium materiality and EJ-09-03 and EJ-09-04 low. Medium judgements were approved by the model owner and the Head of Credit Risk Modelling, low judgements by the model owner, and no proposer approved his or her own judgement. Every medium judgement was challenged before approval by K. Hendriks of Retail Credit Risk Modelling, who is independent of the proposers, and the challenge and its resolution are recorded in the log; the knee-point rule was, for example, challenged against a fixed capture-rate target. No judgement is unquantifiable, and the aggregate effect of all judgements is an increase of the loss allowance by EUR 24.6 million (1.6%) and of the Stage 2 share by 1.8 percentage points against the best statistical alternative, below the high-materiality threshold, so no MRC approval of the aggregate was required. All judgements were reviewed at the 2026 annual review; EJ-09-07 (energy-intensive sectors) was withdrawn with CST-2022-02 and remains in the log as withdrawn.

sections.heading: Stage overrides and management overlays
sections.text: Manual stage overrides are permitted only under the staging override policy in IS-09, which specifies the permitted reasons (SO-01 information on financial difficulty not yet reflected in PD or watchlist, SO-02 sector or regional deterioration identified by Credit Risk Management, SO-03 correction of a documented data error), a maximum change of one stage, the required evidence and the authority levels. Overrides to a lower stage are allowed only under SO-03 with an IT incident reference. Each override records the reason code, a written rationale, the supporting evidence, the proposer and the approver in the Staging Override Tool, and is approved by a credit officer of Credit Risk Management independent of the proposer. Override rates, direction and magnitude are monitored quarterly by portfolio, reason and approving unit under K7. Overlay OVL-2025-02 addresses the specific limitation LIM-09-02, is quantified by an alternative model run applying lifetime ECL with a stressed refinancing PD, and has a remediation plan to integrate an interest-only maturity criterion in model version 2.3 by 31 December 2027. The overlay is recorded in the overlay register with its rationale, the limitation addressed, the affected portfolio and stages, the quantification method, amount, approval and review date, was approved by the Group Impairment Committee on 27 March 2025 after review by Model Validation, and is reassessed quarterly. Because the overlay has been in place for more than four consecutive quarters, the model change assessment MCA-2026-007 under MRM-STD-050 was opened on 10 February 2026.

sections.heading: Purpose and intended use
sections.text: The IFRS 9 SICR and Staging model (MDL-09, model version 2.2) allocates every financial instrument within the IFRS 9 impairment scope to Stage 1, Stage 2 or Stage 3 at each monthly reporting date, and thereby determines whether the loss allowance is measured at 12-month or lifetime expected credit losses. Stage 2 is assigned to every instrument whose credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition, so that lifetime ECL is recognised for these instruments, and Stage 1 is assigned where no such increase has occurred, so that the loss allowance is measured at 12-month ECL. The model is a quantitative method whose output is used for financial reporting and is therefore managed as a model under the Model Risk Management Policy across its full lifecycle, although its core consists of deterministic rules calibrated with expert judgement. It was developed internally by IFRS 9 Modelling and is managed under the Model Risk Management Policy; no vendor component is used. The intended uses are stage allocation for the IFRS 9 loss allowance, the stage breakdown in FINREP and the IFRS 7 disclosures, and, as secondary uses, the Stage 2 ratio in the credit risk appetite dashboard and the identification of Stage 2 exposures in the ICAAP credit risk projections.

sections.heading: Scope of application
sections.text: The model covers financial assets at amortised cost and at fair value through other comprehensive income, lease receivables, loan commitments and financial guarantee contracts of the Bank N.V., its consumer credit subsidiary and its Belgian branch, with a gross carrying amount of EUR 186.2 billion and off-balance exposures of EUR 21.7 billion at 31 December 2026. The portfolios in scope are residential mortgages (EUR 121.6 billion, 548,000 facilities), consumer lending (EUR 6.8 billion, 1.42 million facilities), retail SME (EUR 14.2 billion, 191,000 facilities), corporates (EUR 31.5 billion, 24,600 facilities) and financial institutions, sovereigns and debt securities (EUR 12.1 billion, 1,420 facilities). At 31 December 2026, 88.9% of the gross carrying amount was in Stage 1 (EUR 165.5 billion), 9.4% in Stage 2 (EUR 17.5 billion) and 1.7% in Stage 3 (EUR 3.2 billion), with loss allowances of EUR 212 million, EUR 418 million and EUR 890 million respectively. Purchased or originated credit-impaired assets (EUR 41 million) are identified at initial recognition and are not staged; their loss allowance comprises only the cumulative changes in lifetime ECL since initial recognition. Trade receivables and contract assets under the simplified approach are measured by Finance outside the model and are out of scope.

sections.heading: Users and regulatory use
sections.text: The principal users are Group Reporting and Impairment (Finance), which books the loss allowance, Credit Risk Management, which maintains the watchlist and forbearance inputs and reviews stage overrides, and Risk Reporting, which reports Stage 2 and Stage 3 ratios to the Group Risk Committee. The regulatory use is IFRS 9 financial reporting, including the stage breakdown in FINREP templates F 18.00 and F 12.01; the model is not used for own funds requirements. Stage allocation is not used to take decisions on individual customers: the Privacy Office concluded in DPIA-2024-061 that stage allocation has no legal or similarly significant effect on data subjects, so no automated individual decision within the meaning of Art. 22 GDPR is taken, and the Stage 2 flag does not play a determining role in any customer decision. Known limitations of the model, the conditions of approval and the collective transfers in force are communicated quarterly to Finance and Credit Risk Management through the staging factsheet. The model's Stage 2 ratio is one of the credit risk appetite metrics; the risk parameters behind it are produced by models registered in the model inventory and approved under MRM-POL-001.

sections.heading: Model structure and stage allocation hierarchy
sections.text: Stage allocation is performed monthly at facility level by the staging module of the IFRS 9 calculation engine (ICE), in the following order: (1) POCI assets are excluded from staging; (2) exposures in default under CR-STD-110 are allocated to Stage 3; (3) performing exposures meeting any Stage 2 criterion are allocated to Stage 2; (4) all other exposures are allocated to Stage 1. The Stage 2 criteria are the quantitative lifetime PD criterion (section 4.3), more than 30 days past due on a material amount, forborne performing status, watchlist status, the low credit risk assessment for debt securities, collective Stage 2 transfers and approved manual stage overrides. The criteria combine forward-looking PD information, borrower-specific qualitative information from Credit Risk Management and past-due information, weighted by their relevance for each portfolio through the order of the hierarchy and the portfolio-specific thresholds, so that the assessment is multifactor rather than based on a single indicator. The SICR assessment is performed on the risk of default before the effect of collateral or guarantees; collateral affects the ECL measurement through LGD but not the stage. The model design distinguishes the definition of SICR per exposure type in a clear, documented policy approved by the Group Impairment Committee as part of FIN-STD-200.

sections.heading: Stage 3, credit-impaired assets and definition of default
sections.text: Stage 3 comprises all exposures in default under the prudential definition of default of CR-STD-110, which implements Article 178 CRR, Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 and EBA/GL/2016/07; the IFRS 9 definition of default is therefore identical to the definition used for internal credit risk management. Default is presumed no later than 90 days past due for all portfolios; the Bank does not use a more lagging criterion for any instrument. Credit-impaired assets are identified from observable evidence of events with a detrimental impact on estimated future cash flows, such as significant financial difficulty, a breach of contract or past-due event, concessions granted for reasons of financial difficulty and probable bankruptcy, including the combined effect of several events, all of which are default triggers under CR-STD-110. Stage 3 exposures above EUR 1 million per obligor are measured by the workout function as the difference between the gross carrying amount and the present value of the estimated future cash flows discounted at the original effective interest rate; other Stage 3 exposures use time-in-default LGD models. Definitions of the key terms default, credit-impaired, SICR, Stage 2 and cure are listed in Annex 1 of this document; they are identical for accounting, capital and credit risk management purposes, so no reconciliation of differing definitions is required.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models
sections.text: The model depends on the IFRS 9 PD term structures of the ECL models for residential mortgages (MDL-07), corporates (MDL-08), consumer lending and retail SME, and on the macroeconomic scenarios and probability weights produced by the Macroeconomic Scenario and Satellite Models (MDL-10). The current lifetime PD is the probability-weighted PD over the baseline, upside and downside scenarios approved quarterly by the Group Impairment Committee, so that forward-looking information enters the staging assessment through the PD term structures. The same scenarios and the same PD term structures are used for staging and measurement, and the Stage 2 population is also used in the ICAAP credit risk projections, so that the forward-looking information is consistent across financial reporting, capital planning and management information. The default flag, forbearance status and watchlist status are inputs maintained by Credit Risk Management under CR-STD-110 and CR-POL-001. Upstream model changes are notified to the model owner through the inventory dependency register, and a change of an upstream PD model triggers an assessment of the SICR thresholds.

sections.heading: Segmentation
sections.text: Thresholds are set per portfolio (residential mortgages, consumer lending, retail SME, corporates including financial institutions) and, within each portfolio, per origination PD band, because the significance of a given change in default risk depends on the default risk at initial recognition. The origination PD bands are, for mortgages and corporates, below 0.25% (corporates 0.5%), up to 1.0% (corporates 2.0%) and above; for consumer lending below 1.0%, 1.0% to 3.0% and above; and for retail SME below 1.0% and above. The grouping on portfolio, product and origination PD band is granular enough to assess changes in credit risk: the stage is determined per facility, and the groups are used only to set thresholds, so that group performance cannot obscure increases in credit risk of individual exposures. The segmentation was set by expert judgement EJ-09-01 and confirmed by the calibration results of chapter 5.

sections.heading: Loan commitments, financial guarantees and modifications
sections.text: For loan commitments and financial guarantee contracts, the date on which the Bank became party to the irrevocable commitment is the date of initial recognition, and the origination PD stored at that date is the reference point for the SICR assessment of the commitment and of the drawn exposure that results from it. For modified financial assets that are not derecognised, the risk of default at the reporting date under the modified terms is compared with the risk of default at initial recognition under the original, unmodified terms, which ORIG_RISK retains. The gross carrying amount of such assets is recalculated by Finance as the present value of the modified contractual cash flows discounted at the original effective interest rate, and the modification gain or loss is recognised in profit or loss; the staging model uses the recalculated amount. A modification is not taken as evidence of lower credit risk: modified exposures that are forborne remain in Stage 2 for at least the two-year forborne-performing probation period and return to Stage 1 only after a history of timely payments against the modified terms. The gross carrying amount is written off when there is no reasonable expectation of recovery under the write-off policy of Finance; written-off amounts leave the staging population and the write-off data used in back-testing are consistent with that policy.

The gross carrying amount of such assets is recalculated by Finance as the present value of the modified contractual cash flows discounted at the original effective interest rate, and the modification gain or loss is recognised in profit or loss; the staging model uses the recalculated amount.

A modification is not taken as evidence of lower credit risk: modified exposures that are forborne remain in Stage 2 for at least the two-year forborne-performing probation period and return to Stage 1 only after a history of timely payments against the modified terms.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: The calibration and back-testing data are described in the approved RDS documentation STG-RDS v3.0 (document version 1.0 of 5 March 2027), and the frozen RDS version STG-RDS-v3.0-20270212 is used for all results in this document. The RDS contains 44 quarterly reference dates from March 2015 to December 2025 with twelve-month outcomes up to December 2026, 88.7 million facility-quarter observations and 301,420 default events. The data include information on past events (arrears, defaults, forbearance), current conditions (current PDs and watchlist status) and forecasts (scenario-conditional PD term structures), considered using experienced credit judgement of IFRS 9 Modelling and Credit Risk Management to determine which information is reasonable and supportable. sections.heading: Calibration, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples
sections.text: The samples were defined in the development plan before calibration started: the calibration sample contains the reference dates March 2015 to December 2022 excluding the moratoria quarters (June 2020 to March 2021), the out-of-sample test is a random 30% hold-out of obligors from the same period, and the out-of-time sample contains the reference dates March 2023 to December 2025. The out-of-time sample was not used for the selection of the origination PD bands or for threshold calibration. The samples contain, respectively, 51.2 million, 21.9 million and 15.6 million observations with 176,480, 75,630 and 49,310 default events. The data evaluated cover eleven years, and the historical relationship between PD ratios and defaults is adjusted for current and forecast conditions because the PD term structures themselves are point-in-time and scenario-conditional.

sections.heading: Alternatives considered
sections.text: Four methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (compliance with IFRS 9 and FIN-STD-200, data availability, early default capture, stage stability, interpretability and implementation constraints): (A) relative change in annualised remaining lifetime PD combined with an absolute PD floor; (B) a downgrade of at least three notches on the Bank's master scale; (C) the relative change in 12-month PD only; (D) a statistical transfer model estimating the probability of default within twelve months from the PD ratio, arrears and behavioural variables. Alternative B does not compare risk on a consistent remaining-life basis and is insensitive to forward-looking information for retail pools; alternative C is not compliant with FIN-STD-200 §5.2 for amortising mortgages where default risk is not evenly distributed over the life. Alternative D achieved a two-percentage-point higher capture rate on the out-of-time sample but is less transparent, requires a separate model for each portfolio and would combine a statistical score with stage allocation in a way that is difficult to explain in IFRS 7 disclosures.

sections.heading: Selection rationale
sections.text: Alternative A was selected because it implements the comparison of lifetime default risk required by IFRS 9 paragraph 5.5.9 and FIN-STD-200 §5.2 and §5.3, is transparent, reuses the approved PD term structures and produces stage outcomes that can be reproduced facility by facility. The less transparent alternative D was rejected because its performance gain of two percentage points in capture rate is not sufficient to justify the additional complexity and controls. The three-notch downgrade rule (alternative B) is retained as a benchmark in section 7.4, and the 12-month PD proxy (alternative C) is used only where the conditions of section 4.4 are met. The model is thus a threshold rule applied to model-based PDs; it is not a statistical model with estimated coefficients, and chapter 4 of the template is applied accordingly.

sections.heading: Primary quantitative criterion
sections.text: The SICR assessment performed at each reporting date is based on the change in the risk of a default occurring over the expected life of the instrument, not on the change in the amount of expected credit losses. For each facility, the annualised remaining lifetime PD at the reporting date, PD_cur = 1 − (1 − cumPD_cur(T))^(1/T), is compared with the annualised lifetime PD that was expected at initial recognition for the same remaining term T, PD_orig, taken from the origination PD term structure stored in ORIG_RISK. Comparing annualised PDs for the same remaining term removes the effect of the passage of time on lifetime default risk, so that risk at the reporting date is not simply compared in absolute terms with risk at origination. Both PD_cur and PD_orig are probability-weighted over the macroeconomic scenarios; PD_orig uses the scenarios in force at the origination date. A SICR is identified when the ratio PD_cur/PD_orig exceeds the relative threshold of the portfolio and origination PD band and, in addition, PD_cur − PD_orig exceeds the absolute threshold of the portfolio. The relative change is measured as the ratio of the current to the origination PD, and the absolute change as the difference in percentage points, so both the relative and the absolute change in PD are taken into consideration.

sections.heading: Use of 12-month PD for revolving consumer facilities
sections.text: For credit cards and overdrafts, which have no contractual maturity and a behavioural life of 36 months determined by the consumer lending EAD model, the ratio of current to origination 12-month PD is used as a proxy for the ratio of lifetime PDs. Default patterns of these products are not concentrated at a specific point of the expected life, and there are no circumstances such as balloon repayments that would require a lifetime assessment, so changes in 12-month default risk are a reasonable approximation of changes in lifetime default risk. For credit cards, the stage outcome under the 12-month proxy agreed with the lifetime comparison for 98.7% of facilities and 99.1% of the gross carrying amount at 31 December 2025; this evidence is used for all revolving consumer products. The behavioural life used for the lifetime PD of revolving facilities is the period over which the Bank is exposed to credit risk and ECL would not be mitigated by credit risk management actions, estimated from historical account behaviour, and not the one-month contractual notice period.

sections.heading: Relative and absolute thresholds
sections.text: The relative thresholds decrease with the origination PD band, because a given absolute change in the risk of default is more significant for an instrument originated with a lower risk of default than for one originated with a higher risk. The absolute threshold prevents transfers caused by immaterial PD movements of low-PD exposures, and together with the relative threshold ensures that SICR is not equated with a statistically significant change in PD. Thresholds are calibrated per portfolio as set out in chapter 5, and the threshold values themselves are stored as a version-controlled parameter table in the ICE configuration. The thresholds are applied to all exposures of a portfolio individually; the stage of a facility is therefore not affected by the performance of other facilities in the same group.

sections.heading: Qualitative criteria and backstops
sections.text: Irrespective of the quantitative criterion, the following backstops allocate a performing exposure to Stage 2: more than 30 days past due on a material amount; forborne performing status, for at least the two-year forborne-performing probation period; and inclusion of the obligor on the watchlist. The rebuttable presumption that credit risk has increased significantly when contractual payments are more than 30 days past due is applied to all portfolios as the latest point of transfer, and it is not rebutted for any portfolio. Because the presumption is not rebutted, no analysis demonstrating the absence of correlation between 30 days past due and SICR has been performed or is required; a rebuttal would require a dispensation under FIN-STD-200 §14 supported by such an analysis. The 30 days past due backstop is used alongside the earlier PD, watchlist and forbearance indicators and not as the primary indicator: in 2026 only 9.8% of defaulted facilities had reached Stage 2 through the backstop alone. The watchlist criterion reflects the early-warning indicators of CR-POL-001 §10.1, which include covenant breaches, significant changes in the borrower's operating results, external rating downgrades and adverse sector information, and therefore captures qualitative indicators of increased credit risk that the PD does not reflect. The SICR assessment is not based solely on quantitative analysis.

sections.heading: Collective assessment and collective Stage 2 transfers
sections.text: Where evidence of a significant increase in credit risk is not yet available at facility level, SICR is assessed collectively for groups of exposures sharing credit risk characteristics, using information indicative of increased credit risk for those groups. Each collective transfer specifies the affected population, the triggering evidence and its review date, and is approved by the Group Impairment Committee together with the associated overlay. Collective transfer CST-2025-01 transfers to Stage 2 the interest-only residential mortgages with an indexed loan-to-value above 80% and a contractual maturity before 2037 (EUR 2.4 billion, 21,300 facilities), because refinancing risk at maturity is not reflected in the behavioural PD; it corresponds to overlay OVL-2025-02 of EUR 11.8 million, so that stage allocation and measurement are consistent. Where a sub-group with increased credit risk cannot be identified precisely, the transfer is applied to the portion of the group for which credit risk is deemed to have increased significantly, as delimited by the loan-to-value and maturity criteria. No other collective transfer is in force at 31 December 2026; the transfer CST-2022-02 for energy-intensive corporate sectors was withdrawn on 30 September 2024.

sections.heading: Low credit risk exemption
sections.text: The low credit risk exemption is applied only to debt securities with an internal rating equivalent to investment grade (internal grades 1 to 10 on the 22-grade master scale, equivalent to BBB− or better) and is not applied to loans and advances. The internal rating reflects a low risk of default and a strong capacity of the issuer to meet its contractual cash flow obligations in the near term, assessed without reliance on collateral and not merely relative to other exposures of the Bank or to the issuer's jurisdiction. Low credit risk is evaluated primarily on the internal rating; an external investment-grade rating does not qualify an instrument automatically, and where the internal rating is more favourable than the external rating the difference is justified in the credit file. At 31 December 2026 the exemption applies to 318 debt securities with a carrying amount of EUR 9.4 billion, all rated in internal grades 1 to 6. A debt security that ceases to qualify as low credit risk is not transferred to Stage 2 automatically; the quantitative criterion is then applied against its PD at initial recognition.

sections.heading: Transfer back to Stage 1 and exit from Stage 3
sections.text: An exposure returns from Stage 2 to Stage 1 when none of the Stage 2 criteria is met at the reporting date, so that the loss allowance is again measured at 12-month ECL; no probation applies beyond the forborne-performing probation period. Exposures leave Stage 3 only after completion of the probation period defined in CR-STD-110 (three months, or twelve months after a distressed restructuring), after which they are allocated to Stage 2 if they are forborne performing or meet another Stage 2 criterion. A decrease in allowance following a renegotiation or modification requires a consistently satisfactory payment performance over the forborne-performing probation period of at least two years. The effectiveness of this symmetrical treatment is monitored through the stage reversal KPI of section 10.1: in 2026, 17.3% of facilities transferred to Stage 2 returned to Stage 1 within six months.

sections.heading: Origination PD for legacy facilities
sections.text: For facilities originated before origination PDs were stored (mortgages before 2008, retail SME before 2012, corporates before 2010), the origination PD is proxied by the PD of the earliest archived rating adjusted to the origination date with the average migration between origination and first rating (EJ-09-03). Legacy facilities represent 14.8% of mortgage, 9.6% of retail SME and 3.1% of corporate facilities at 31 December 2026. The impact of the proxy on stage allocation was analysed against an alternative proxy without migration adjustment: the Stage 2 share of legacy facilities changes from 7.1% to 7.6% for mortgages and from 9.9% to 10.4% for retail SME, with a combined impact on the loss allowance of EUR 3.0 million. The proxy is recorded as limitation LIM-09-04 and its share declines by roughly one percentage point per year as legacy facilities mature.

sections.heading: Calibration target and method
sections.text: The calibration target is the trade-off between early default capture and stage volatility: for each portfolio and origination PD band, a grid of relative thresholds (1.25 to 4.0 in steps of 0.05) and absolute thresholds (0.05 to 2.0 percentage points in steps of 0.05) is evaluated on the calibration sample. For each grid point the capture rate (share of defaults allocated to Stage 2 at least six months before default), the Stage 2 share of the performing gross carrying amount and the stage reversal rate are computed. The selected thresholds lie at the point of the trade-off curve beyond which one additional percentage point of Stage 2 share adds less than one percentage point of capture rate, subject to a stage reversal rate below 25%; this knee-point rule is expert judgement EJ-09-06. The calibration is re-assessed at least annually during the annual model review.

sections.heading: Calibrated thresholds
sections.text: The thresholds in force from model version 2.2 are as follows. Residential mortgages: relative threshold 3.0 for origination PD below 0.25%, 2.5 from 0.25% to below 1.0% and 2.0 from 1.0%, with an absolute threshold of 0.20 percentage points. Consumer lending: relative threshold 2.25 for origination PD below 1.0%, 1.9 from 1.0% to below 3.0% and 1.6 from 3.0%, with an absolute threshold of 0.75 percentage points (0.0075 in PD units). Retail SME: relative threshold 2.5 for origination PD below 1.0% and 2.0 from 1.0%, with an absolute threshold of 0.50 percentage points; corporates and financial institutions: relative threshold 3.0 below 0.5%, 2.5 from 0.5% to below 2.0% and 2.0 from 2.0%, with an absolute threshold of 0.40 percentage points. On the calibration sample these thresholds capture 72.8% (mortgages), 64.1% (consumer lending), 65.0% (retail SME) and 67.9% (corporates) of defaults at least six months before default, at Stage 2 shares of 6.3%, 12.6%, 10.2% and 8.8% of the performing gross carrying amount. The mortgage, retail SME and corporate thresholds were re-assessed quantitatively in 2027 and remain unchanged from version 2.0, because the knee point moved by less than one grid step.

sections.heading: Recalibration of the consumer lending thresholds
sections.text: The 2026 staging back-test showed an amber capture rate of 58.2% for consumer lending, caused by the shift of the consumer portfolio towards lower origination PDs after the 2024 credit card limit policy change. The consumer lending thresholds were therefore recalibrated on the calibration sample extended to December 2022: the relative thresholds changed from 2.5, 2.0 and 1.75 to 2.25, 1.9 and 1.6, and the absolute threshold from 1.00 to 0.75 percentage points. On the out-of-time sample the recalibrated thresholds increase the consumer capture rate from 58.9% to 64.9%, raise the consumer Stage 2 share from 11.2% to 12.6% and keep the stage reversal rate at 21.4%. The change is documented in change memorandum CHG-2027-031, classified as non-material, and increases the total loss allowance by EUR 6.3 million (0.4%) at 31 December 2026.

sections.heading: Margin of conservatism
sections.text: Not applicable. The staging model produces an unbiased stage allocation for IFRS 9 purposes, and FIN-STD-200 §4.1 excludes prudential conservatism from IFRS 9 models: no margin of conservatism, downturn component or regulatory floor is applied to the thresholds or to the PD inputs used for staging. Where the upstream PD term structures are derived from IRB parameters, the removal of MoC and downturn components and the TTC-to-PIT conversion are documented, justified and quantified in the MDDs of the PD models, and the staging model uses only the resulting IFRS 9 PDs. Uncertainty in the thresholds is addressed through the sensitivity analysis of section 7.5 and, where a risk is not captured, through overlays under FIN-STD-200 §10 rather than conservatism in the thresholds.

sections.heading: Performance metrics and thresholds
sections.text: Performance is measured on the calibration, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples by the capture rate (discriminatory power of the staging rule for defaults six or more months ahead), the Stage 1 direct-to-default share, the backstop-only share, the stage reversal rate and the population stability of the SICR ratio. The acceptance thresholds, set in the monitoring plan and approved by MRM because MV-HB-003 contains no specific staging tests, are: capture rate green from 60%, amber from 45%; Stage 1 direct-to-default green up to 25%, amber up to 35%; backstop-only share green up to 15%, amber up to 25%; stage reversal green up to 25%, amber up to 35%; PSI green below 0.10 and red above 0.25. The discriminatory power of the SICR ratio for defaults in the following twelve months, measured by the AUC, is 0.84 for mortgages, 0.79 for consumer lending, 0.77 for retail SME and 0.74 for corporates on the out-of-time sample, compared with 0.85, 0.80, 0.78 and 0.75 on the calibration sample. Where performance thresholds are significantly breached, the monitoring plan requires remedial action up to recalibration of the thresholds or redevelopment of the staging rule.

sections.heading: Staging back-testing results
sections.text: Back-testing of stage allocation is performed annually on the defaults of the preceding calendar year. For defaults in 2026, the share of defaulted facilities that were in Stage 2 at least six months before default was 71.4% for mortgages, 58.2% for consumer lending, 63.5% for retail SME and 66.7% for corporates, 59.5% in total by count; 22.4% of defaults came directly from Stage 1 and 9.8% had reached Stage 2 through the 30 days past due backstop alone. The frequency of stage reversals, measured as the share of Stage 2 inflows returning to Stage 1 within six months, was 17.3%. The amber consumer lending result was analysed for its cause (portfolio shift towards lower origination PDs), recorded as limitation LIM-09-11 and addressed by the recalibration of section 5.3; with the recalibrated thresholds the 2026 consumer capture rate would have been 64.9%. The back-test results are consistent with the direction of observable data: the Stage 2 share increased from 8.7% to 9.4% in 2026 as unemployment rose from 3.7% to 4.1% and arrears in consumer lending increased.

sections.heading: Performance by segment
sections.text: Performance is reported for the whole model and for each portfolio and origination PD band on the out-of-time sample. In the out-of-time period 2023–2025, capture rates by band range from 61% to 78% for mortgages, 57% to 69% for consumer lending (before recalibration), 59% to 70% for retail SME and 60% to 74% for corporates; the lowest capture rates occur in the highest origination PD band of each portfolio, where defaults are more often sudden. The Stage 2 share by band ranges from 3.9% (mortgages below 0.25%) to 31.2% (consumer lending from 3.0%). The four consumer lending bands below 60% were analysed and recorded in the limitations log, and the recalibration addresses them. The capture rate for the financial institutions and debt securities portfolio cannot be computed because of the absence of defaults; for these exposures performance is assessed qualitatively through the rating migration of the obligors.

sections.heading: Benchmarking
sections.text: As a Tier 2 model, the staging model is compared with two benchmarks: the previous model version 2.1 and the three-notch downgrade rule (alternative B). On the 2023–2025 out-of-time sample, version 2.2 captures 66.1% of defaults six months ahead with a Stage 2 share of 9.1%, version 2.1 captures 64.4% at 8.8% and the three-notch rule 57.3% at 7.9%. The difference to the three-notch rule arises mainly in retail portfolios, where master-scale notches are coarse and the rule ignores the scenario-dependent PD term structure; the benchmark does not outperform the model on any material metric. The statistical transfer model (alternative D) captured 68.1% at a Stage 2 share of 9.3%, a difference that is explained in section 4.1 and does not justify its complexity.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions, parameters and input data: thresholds shifted by one grid step up and down, the calibration window with and without the 2015 approximated defaults and the moratoria quarters, the alternative legacy origination PD proxy, and the 12-month PD proxy for revolving facilities. A shift of all relative thresholds by +0.25 reduces the Stage 2 share from 9.4% to 8.3% and the loss allowance by EUR 38 million; a shift by −0.25 increases them to 10.8% and by EUR 47 million. Including the moratoria quarters in the calibration objective would raise the selected consumer relative threshold in the middle band from 1.9 to 2.0 and reduce the loss allowance by EUR 2.1 million; excluding the 2015 reference dates changes no threshold. Under a 100% weight on the downside scenario of MDL-10 the Stage 2 share rises to 13.1% and the loss allowance by EUR 108 million, and under a 100% weight on the upside scenario the Stage 2 share falls to 7.8% and the loss allowance by EUR 84 million, which demonstrates how stage allocation and ECL change with the scenarios. Because the calibration window contains no severe housing downturn, a stress test of the mortgage thresholds on the 2009–2013 approximated data shows a capture rate of 69%, close to the calibration result.

sections.heading: Consistency with ECL measurement and loss experience
sections.text: The ECL measurement method for each portfolio is the PD/LGD/EAD approach of the respective ECL model, with discounted cash flows for individually assessed Stage 3 exposures; the staging model determines only whether 12-month or lifetime ECL is measured. Twelve-month ECL is measured as the lifetime cash shortfalls resulting from a default within twelve months after the reporting date weighted by that default probability, not as the cash shortfalls expected over the next twelve months; the staging flag selects the corresponding PD horizon in ICE. ECL is calculated separately per scenario and probability-weighted, which reflects both the possibility that a credit loss occurs and the possibility that none occurs, and is discounted to the reporting date at the effective interest rate. The annual review compares the loss allowance of Stage 2 exposures with realised credit losses and write-offs; the methodology and thresholds are reviewed to reduce differences between estimates and loss experience. The ECL horizon for Stage 2 facilities does not exceed the maximum contractual period, including extension options, except for revolving facilities, for which the behavioural period of section 4.4 applies.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: All material assumptions were identified and assessed for plausibility: (a) the PD term structures of the upstream models are accurate and point-in-time; (b) the relationship between PD ratio and subsequent default observed in 2015–2025 remains stable; (c) watchlist and forbearance flags are complete and timely; (d) the origination PD proxy for legacy facilities is unbiased; (e) the 12-month PD ratio is a reasonable proxy for revolving facilities. Assumption (a) is supported by the annual back-testing of the PD models, (b) by the stable AUC between calibration and out-of-time samples, (c) by the DQ results in the RDS documentation, (d) by the sensitivity analysis of section 4.10 and (e) by the agreement analysis of section 4.4. The staging model assumes that credit risk management actions such as limit reductions do not mitigate ECL within the behavioural life, consistent with the EAD model.

sections.heading: Implementation specification and handover
sections.text: The implementation specification IS-09 v2.2, approved by the model owner on 20 April 2027, is consistent with this MDD and defines every input and its production source field and lineage, the stage hierarchy, the threshold parameter table with four-decimal precision, the fallback rules and the override interface. The handover package to Finance Risk IT contained the implementation specification, the final threshold table, 1,240 test cases with expected stage outcomes produced with the development code, covering typical cases, boundary values at each threshold, missing and invalid inputs and every portfolio and origination PD band, and reference outputs for the full portfolio at 31 December 2026. The implementation and its testing are documented in the implementation and testing report EVD-09-IMPL, and production use of version 2.2 starts only after testing, reconciliation, the parallel run and UAT have been completed. The development and production lineage were compared: both read the same FRDP tables, and the difference in the legacy product mapping has no effect on outputs.

sections.heading: Production controls
sections.text: Production and development code are held in the approved version control system; the staging module is released from the repository ifrs9/ice-staging with tag 2.2.0, and the threshold table is a version-controlled, access-restricted parameter file changed only through change management. Model developers in IFRS 9 Modelling have read-only access to the production environment; deployments are performed by Finance Risk IT after four-eyes code review by a person other than the author and documented approval. Each production run logs the reference date, the input data version, the code version and the parameter table version, and the engine refuses to start if the parameter version differs from the approved version in the release register. Manual reruns and the fallback allocation to Stage 2 for facilities without a current PD are documented in the run book, authorised by the Head of Impairment Reporting and logged. Stage outputs used for regulatory reporting are retained for ten years together with the input data and code version used to produce them.
